options.text: Use a predictable, brief goodbye and maintain consistent comforting care and familiar routines while the caregiver is away.
options.reason: Predictability and responsive care support trust during separation anxiety.
options.label: B

options.text: Have the caregiver leave secretly whenever the infant looks away.
options.reason: Unexplained disappearance can undermine predictability and does not teach security.
options.label: C

options.text: Place the infant alone and avoid comforting to prevent dependence.
options.reason: Responsive comfort is appropriate in infancy and supports trust.
options.label: D

rationale: Separation anxiety is developmentally expected. The nursing response should support attachment and predictable care rather than punish distress.

stem: A 2-year-old requires an oral medication and becomes upset whenever the nurse enters. Which approaches support cooperation and safe care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explain in simple words immediately before administration and allow comforting caregiver participation.
options.reason: Toddlers respond to concrete, immediate explanations and familiar support.
options.label: A

options.text: Ask, "Do you want your medicine?" when refusing is not an available option.
options.reason: This offers a false choice and increases conflict.
options.label: B

options.text: Describe the medicine as candy so the child accepts it.
options.reason: Calling medication candy creates poisoning risk and undermines honest teaching.
options.label: C

options.text: Mix the dose into a full bottle and assume the entire dose was taken.
options.reason: Incomplete intake makes the delivered dose uncertain.
options.label: D

options.text: Offer two acceptable choices, such as taking the medicine with the caregiver or with the nurse.
options.reason: Limited real choices support autonomy without making necessary treatment optional.
options.label: E

rationale: Support autonomy within safe limits. Honest explanations, limited choices, and an accurate dose are more useful than coercion or deception.

stem: A 4-year-old awaiting a procedure says, "My arm got hurt because I was mean to my brother." Which nursing response is best?

options.text: Explain that the injury was not punishment and use a doll to show what will happen during care.
options.reason: Preschool magical thinking can link illness to behavior; concrete play helps correct the misconception.
options.label: A

options.text: Confirm that better behavior will make the arm heal faster.
options.reason: This reinforces guilt and an inaccurate cause of illness.
options.label: B

options.text: Provide a detailed discussion of cellular inflammation and ask for a written summary.
options.reason: This is not matched to preschool cognitive abilities.
options.label: C

options.text: Avoid discussing the procedure because preschoolers cannot understand any explanation.
options.reason: Simple truthful preparation and play can reduce fear.
options.label: D

rationale: Address the child's actual belief. Developmentally appropriate preparation includes reassurance about causation and concrete demonstration.

stem: A hospitalized 10-year-old says, "Everyone else can do things. I am bad at everything now." Which care plan best supports the child's developmental needs?

options.text: Teach a manageable self-care skill, recognize progress, and help maintain appropriate school and peer contact.
options.reason: Achievable tasks and connection support industry and competence.
options.label: A

options.text: Compare the child's progress with a faster-recovering roommate.
options.reason: Competitive comparison can intensify feelings of inferiority.
options.label: B

options.text: Explain that peers are unimportant until adolescence.
options.reason: Peer relationships are already important in school-age development.
options.label: C

options.text: Complete every task for the child to avoid any possibility of failure.
options.reason: Removing all participation can reinforce inferiority and dependence.
options.label: D

rationale: School-age children benefit from meaningful participation and achievable success, not loss of all responsibility or unfavorable comparison.

stem: A caregiver says, "My 2-year-old goes up stairs one step at a time while holding the railing, so I removed the stair gate and let the child practice alone." Which response is best?

options.text: Explain that emerging stair skills do not establish independent safety; continue close supervision and appropriate barriers.
options.reason: The skill can fit the developmental period, but judgment, balance, and hazard awareness remain immature.
options.label: A

options.text: Agree that one successful climb means supervision is no longer needed.
options.reason: Demonstrating a skill once does not eliminate fall risk.
options.label: B

options.text: Diagnose a developmental delay because alternating feet are required at age 2.
options.reason: Alternating-foot stair use develops later; this description alone does not establish delay.
options.label: C

options.text: Tell the caregiver to discourage all climbing until school age.
options.reason: Safe supervised practice supports development; complete avoidance is unnecessary.
options.label: D

rationale: Developmental ability and safety readiness are not identical. Teach protection while allowing appropriate supervised learning.

stem: The nurse reviews two healthy patients with no vaccine contraindications. A 4-year-old received all routine doses through 18 months but none of the 4-6-year boosters. An 18-year-old entering a college residence hall received MenACWY only at age 11. Which plans are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Plan the 4-year-old's final routine IPV dose after checking minimum intervals.
options.reason: The final routine IPV dose is given at age 4 years or older with the required interval.
options.label: A

options.text: Plan the 4-year-old's second MMR and varicella doses.
options.reason: These are routine 4-6-year doses for a child with the stated earlier series.
options.label: B

options.text: Use a MenB dose as a substitute for the college student's missing MenACWY booster.
options.reason: MenB and MenACWY cover different serogroups and are not interchangeable.
options.label: C

options.text: Plan a MenACWY dose for the college student.
options.reason: A dose given only at age 11 does not provide the recommended later adolescent booster coverage.
options.label: D

options.text: Plan the 4-year-old's DTaP booster after verifying the documented doses and intervals.
options.reason: The routine DTaP series includes a 4-6-year booster when the earlier doses were given as described.
options.label: E

options.text: Restart the 4-year-old's completed hepatitis B series because kindergarten is approaching.
options.reason: A completed valid series is not restarted merely for school entry.
options.label: F

rationale: Reconcile actual records before vaccinating. Age, prior valid doses, and intervals determine the plan; MenB counseling is a separate decision from completing MenACWY protection.

stem: During anticipatory guidance for a 10-year-old, which caregiver statement most clearly requires correction?

options.text: "We use a helmet on every bicycle ride, including short rides."
options.reason: Consistent helmet use supports injury prevention.
options.label: A

options.text: "We review an emergency contact plan before allowing time at home without me."
options.reason: Planning and assessment of readiness support safer independence.
options.label: B

options.text: "We check who supervises swimming rather than assuming another adult is watching."
options.reason: Defined active supervision reduces water-injury risk.
options.label: C

options.text: "My child wears a seat belt correctly, so the front passenger seat is as safe as the back seat."
options.reason: Children younger than 13 should ride in the back seat; proper belt fit does not eliminate front-airbag risk.
options.label: D

rationale: Independence should increase with development while evidence-based protection remains in place. Correct the specific unsafe practice rather than discouraging all autonomy.

stem: A child with localized impetigo has used prescribed topical mupirocin for two days. Today the lesions are spreading, the surrounding skin is warm and tender, and the child has fever. What should the nurse advise?

options.text: Stop all antibiotics because crusting means the infection has resolved.
options.reason: Spreading lesions and fever contradict resolution.
options.label: A

options.text: Replace the antibiotic with a potent topical steroid to suppress redness.
options.reason: Steroid monotherapy does not treat the infection and can mask progression.
options.label: B

options.text: Arrange prompt reassessment for spreading infection and possible need for systemic therapy.
options.reason: New systemic symptoms and expanding inflammation suggest that the original localized-treatment plan may be inadequate.
options.label: C

options.text: Increase the topical amount without contacting the prescriber.
options.reason: Dose escalation alone does not evaluate spreading infection or determine whether systemic treatment is needed.
options.label: D

rationale: Treatment response must be evaluated by the whole clinical trend. New fever and spreading inflammation require a revised assessment.

stem: A child was treated for head lice yesterday with a product that specifies repeat treatment on day 9. No live crawling lice are seen, but attached nits remain. The caregiver asks to apply the product twice daily until every nit is gone. Which response is best?

options.text: Follow the product's retreatment schedule, remove nits as directed, and reassess for live lice rather than overapplying medication.
options.reason: Retreatment timing is product-specific; remaining nits alone do not justify excessive dosing.
options.label: A

options.text: Apply two different lice products together to overcome presumed resistance.
options.reason: Combining products can increase toxicity and should not be done without clinical guidance.
options.label: B

options.text: Stop checking the hair permanently because one treatment always kills all eggs.
options.reason: Products differ in egg activity, and follow-up may still be needed.
options.label: C

options.text: Use household insecticide spray on the child's scalp between doses.
options.reason: Environmental insecticide sprays are unsafe for treating a child's scalp.
options.label: D

rationale: Avoid mistaking residual nits for proof of immediate treatment failure. Use the actual product instructions and assess living lice before escalating treatment.

stem: A child with scabies has prescribed permethrin treatment. Several household members have itching, and others have no symptoms. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Treat household furniture with pesticide foggers while the child remains in the home.
options.reason: Fumigants are not recommended and create unnecessary toxic exposure.
options.label: A

options.text: Reapply the medication every few hours whenever any itching remains.
options.reason: Itching can persist after successful treatment; excessive application increases harm.
options.label: B

options.text: Arrange treatment of household and close contacts together as directed, including eligible contacts without symptoms.
options.reason: Symptoms may be delayed, and untreated contacts can cause reinfestation.
options.label: C

options.text: Wash recently used clothing, towels, and bedding with hot washing and drying, or seal unwashable items for the recommended interval.
options.reason: Environmental measures reduce re-exposure from recently used items.
options.label: D

options.text: Apply the child's prescribed product to the instructed areas for the full instructed contact time.
options.reason: Coverage, age-specific application, and duration affect treatment success.
options.label: E

options.text: Report new burrows, worsening lesions, or signs of skin infection after treatment.
options.reason: These findings can indicate ongoing infestation or a complication requiring reassessment.
options.label: F

rationale: Successful scabies control combines correct medication use, contact management, and practical cleaning. Persistent itch alone does not prove that mites survived.

stem: A child with atopic dermatitis has very dry skin and worsening itch. The caregiver gives long hot baths and applies a prescribed topical corticosteroid over the entire body every day, including clear skin. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop all moisturizers so that inflamed areas can dry completely.
options.reason: Drying worsens barrier dysfunction and itching.
options.label: A

options.text: Scrub with an antibacterial brush before each steroid application.
options.reason: Friction and harsh cleansing can worsen inflammation and skin injury.
options.label: B

options.text: Increase the steroid strength without evaluation when the child scratches.
options.reason: Potency, location, age, and duration must be considered by the prescribing clinician.
options.label: C

options.text: Use brief lukewarm bathing, apply emollient promptly, and use the corticosteroid only as prescribed for affected areas.
options.reason: This supports the skin barrier while limiting unnecessary corticosteroid exposure.
options.label: D

rationale: Control eczema by restoring the barrier and using targeted anti-inflammatory treatment. More heat, friction, or steroid is not automatically better care.

stem: An adolescent with psoriasis says the plaques are improving but reports new persistent swelling and stiffness in several finger joints. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Apply the skin cream directly over the joints as the only intervention.
options.reason: Topical skin treatment does not adequately evaluate or manage inflammatory joint disease.
options.label: A

options.text: Report the joint symptoms and arrange evaluation for possible psoriatic arthritis.
options.reason: Psoriasis can involve joints even when the skin appears to improve.
options.label: B

options.text: Reassure the adolescent that joint symptoms cannot be related to a skin disorder.
options.reason: This dismisses a recognized extra-cutaneous manifestation.
options.label: C

options.text: Recommend avoiding school because psoriasis is contagious.
options.reason: Psoriasis is not contagious, and unnecessary exclusion adds stigma.
options.label: D

rationale: Evaluate the patient beyond visible lesions. Improvement in one part of a chronic condition does not exclude progression elsewhere.

stem: A 5-week-old has progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting, weight loss, and a palpable olive-like abdominal mass. Potassium is 2.9 mEq/L and bicarbonate is elevated. Pyloromyotomy is planned. Which preoperative priority should the nurse expect?

options.text: Give an oral potassium dose and send the infant directly to surgery without reassessment.
options.reason: The route and stabilization plan must account for vomiting, hydration, and safe electrolyte correction.
options.label: A

options.text: Feed concentrated formula to restore weight rapidly before transfer to the operating room.
options.reason: Oral feeding worsens vomiting and aspiration risk before correction of the obstruction.
options.label: B

options.text: Maintain NPO status and correct dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities with the prescribed IV plan before anesthesia.
options.reason: Pyloric obstruction causes losses that must be stabilized for safer surgery.
options.label: C

options.text: Delay IV access because metabolic alkalosis is a normal infant finding.
options.reason: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and dehydration are clinically important complications.
options.label: D

rationale: Definitive surgery is necessary, but the physiologic deficits require correction first when clinically feasible. A surgical diagnosis does not erase resuscitation priorities.

stem: A child awaiting appendectomy reports sudden relief of right-lower-quadrant pain. Thirty minutes later, the abdomen is rigid, pain is generalized, and the pulse is rising. Which action has priority?

options.text: Offer a meal because the original focal pain has improved.
options.reason: Oral intake is unsafe with a potential surgical emergency.
options.label: A

options.text: Notify the surgical team immediately about possible perforation and support the prescribed NPO, IV, and antibiotic plan.
options.reason: Transient relief followed by generalized peritoneal findings suggests progression, not recovery.
options.label: B

options.text: Apply a heating pad to reduce abdominal muscle tension.
options.reason: Heat is not appropriate for suspected appendiceal perforation and may delay definitive care.
options.label: C

options.text: Give a cleansing enema before reassessing the abdomen.
options.reason: Enemas can worsen risk in suspected appendicitis and are not appropriate treatment.
options.label: D

rationale: Interpret pain changes over time. Sudden relief can precede worsening peritonitis; it is not automatically a successful outcome.

stem: A stable 9-month-old with confirmed intussusception is being prepared for air-enema reduction. Before transfer, the child becomes lethargic, febrile, and hypotensive, with a rigid abdomen. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed with the enema because it was ordered before the assessment changed.
options.reason: Orders must be reconsidered when the patient's condition changes materially.
options.label: A

options.text: Stop the routine transfer plan and urgently notify the team about possible perforation or peritonitis while supporting circulation.
options.reason: New instability and peritoneal signs may make enema reduction unsafe and require urgent surgical management.
options.label: B

options.text: Give an oral rehydration solution and repeat vital signs after the procedure.
options.reason: Shock and a possible perforation require IV resuscitation and reassessment before the procedure.
options.label: C

options.text: Wait for currant-jelly stool to confirm that intussusception is serious.
options.reason: The classic stool can be late or absent; current shock is sufficient reason to escalate.
options.label: D

rationale: Reassess suitability immediately before an intervention. A treatment appropriate for a stable child may be unsafe after deterioration.

stem: The pediatric nurse receives four GI-related reports. Which child requires the first bedside assessment?

options.text: A child with treated constipation who passes a soft stool without blood and has normal vital signs.
options.reason: This suggests a response to the current plan rather than acute deterioration.
options.label: A

options.text: An infant with uncomplicated reflux who is gaining weight and sleeps supine on a firm, flat surface.
options.reason: Growth and safe sleep are reassuring in this report; reflux does not require prone or inclined sleep.
options.label: B

options.text: An infant with Hirschsprung disease who now has fever, increasing distention, explosive diarrhea, and poor perfusion.
options.reason: This suggests Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis with possible sepsis; diarrhea does not exclude obstructive disease.
options.label: C

options.text: A child after successful intussusception reduction who is alert, pain-free, and has normal perfusion.
options.reason: Continued monitoring is required, but this report is stable compared with suspected enterocolitis.
options.label: D

rationale: Prioritize systemic illness and impaired perfusion over diagnostic labels. In Hirschsprung disease, new diarrhea can be a danger sign rather than relief of constipation.

stem: A caregiver calls after finding a toddler beside an open acetaminophen bottle. The amount and time of possible ingestion are uncertain; the child is currently awake and breathing normally. Which instructions or anticipated care are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Seek emergency help immediately if the child becomes difficult to awaken, has a seizure, or develops breathing difficulty.
options.reason: These findings require emergency services and stabilization.
options.label: A

options.text: Expect the evaluation to consider timed acetaminophen levels and N-acetylcysteine when indicated.
options.reason: Levels and the exposure history guide care; N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen toxicity.
options.label: B

options.text: Give syrup of ipecac now to empty the stomach before symptoms begin.
options.reason: Induced vomiting is not recommended and can cause harm or delay effective treatment.
options.label: C

options.text: Wait for abdominal pain or jaundice before calling because the child appears well.
options.reason: Significant acetaminophen toxicity can initially cause few symptoms.
options.label: D

options.text: Contact Poison Control promptly with the bottle, possible amount, timing, and child's weight, and follow its urgent evaluation instructions.
options.reason: Early symptoms may be absent despite a toxic exposure; expert guidance should not be delayed.
options.label: E

rationale: Assess and act on exposure risk, not appearance alone. Activated charcoal, when indicated, is a separate decontamination treatment and is not the antidote.
